     "subtitle": "History outside academic salons: New media and the importance of archival material",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim in the studio explains the importance of new media and researching archival material in contemporary historiography.",
     "content": "In the Zagreb studio of the show *Pogled s Markovog trga*, the host welcomes the young historian **Krešimir Rotim**, pointing out in the introduction that his work is recognizable for having successfully pulled history out of closed academic salons and university chairs and transferred it into the *mainstream* and under the spotlights. While the public is used to older historians who speak at length and broadly, Rotim has stood out with short and concise formats in the new media, and this guest appearance is an opportunity for a deeper and more extensive analysis of complex historical topics.\n\nExplaining his transition toward new media formats, Rotim states that he himself was part of the academic community, studied history, and went through a multitude of scientific articles and books. During that process, he noticed that certain arguments and narratives simply do not break through to the public. Guided by the legal principle *let the other side be heard as well*, he realized that modern technologies have changed the way of communication. While once the main means of fighting for the truth was the pen, today it is short videos and longer-form shows that allow for the presentation of in-depth analysis.\n\nRotim emphasizes that his views stem from accumulated knowledge and, what is most important for a historian, from **archival material**. In contrast, he claims that *mainstream* historians do not work that way, but rather try to constantly keep Croats in a tense atmosphere of guilt. As a blatant example of such an approach, he singles out the public debate between **Igor Vukić** and **Ivo Goldstein**:\n\n- Instead of a serious scientific discussion, Goldstein trivialized a first-rate geopolitical, security, and historiographical question with a story about a \"crusher\".\n- By doing so, according to Rotim's words, he showed the actual reach of his decades-long scientific research.\n\nNew media therefore represent a key opportunity for people to feel that history is not as it has been presented to them for decades, but that there is also an argument-based Croatian side of history.",

    {
     "subtitle": "The stigma of revisionism and the absence of dialogue on the contemporary left",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim speaks about revision as the foundation of every science and the lack of readiness for public debate among historians on the left.",
     "content": "The host opens the question of why, after 36 years of Croatian independence, the historical paradigm is still strongly permeated, and even reinforced, by a Yugoslav narrative that is almost identical to the Serbian *mainstream*. He calls such a state auto-chauvinism and a pathology that leads to psychological warfare, reminding how the actions of Television Belgrade and Belgrade media in the nineties directly led to war, while today similar patterns can be seen all the way to the recent actions of **Lordan Zafranović**. In that context, the question is raised as to why revision is desirable in all sciences, while in Croatian historiography the term \"revisionist\" is used as the worst accusation, almost at the level of an enemy of the state and the party of **Comrade Tito**.\n\nRotim points out that revision is actually the foundation of every science, and especially history, which is extremely burdened by politicization from the period of the Second World War, the post-war era, and communism. He reminds that **Stalin** consciously, in order to defend the Soviet regime, introduced the concept of anti-fascism and thereby contaminated the entire discussion that lasts to this day. Because of this, today it is difficult to make an objective overview of the way Bolshevism viewed fascism before it cunningly crossed over to the side of the Western Allies and thus morally legitimized itself in victory.\n\nLabeling someone as a revisionist is, for Rotim, exclusively a **method of disqualification** used by the media with their soft power and by certain historians in order to push dissenters out of the public space. The goal of his public activity is precisely removing that stigma and breaking the famous \"Croatian silence\". Speaking about personal attacks and professional defamations he faces, Rotim reveals:\n\n- Creative insults coming from eastern neighbors mostly make him laugh, but it is unpleasant when someone tries to professionally defame him without readiness for a direct confrontation.\n- **Hrvoje Klasić** refused a public confrontation, and Rotim considers that after Goldstein's experience, no one else from that side will even dare to come to a debate.\n\nRotim emphasizes that his approach is not scandalizing the public, but researching according to the principle *sine ira et studio* (without hatred and bias) in order to remove the horror propaganda from certain periods of the Croatian past. It particularly saddens him that today's left has become intellectually lazy; while once it was inclined toward discussions and mental effort from which progress stems, today among them he sees no serious historians capable of coming out to a public debate and talking in a democratic spirit about national interests.",

     "subtitle": "Continuity of Serbian politics: From the December Victims to the Banovina of Croatia",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim explains the political circumstances after the establishment of the Banovina of Croatia and the plans of the Chetnik movement.",
     "content": "Analyzing the broader context of the 20th century, the host refers to conversations with Dr. **Tihomir Rajčić**, an expert on Serbian politics up to the First World War, pointing out that there is a clear continuity of Greater Serbian ideas from the period before the First World War, through the interwar period in the Kingdom of SHS and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, all the way to the nineties and the present day. He emphasizes that history must not be viewed in fragments, starting only from the Second World War, but one needs to understand what preceded it. As a key point, he singles out **August 26, 1939**, when the **Banovina of Croatia** was created by the **Cvetković-Maček** agreement, which immediately provoked resistance from Serbian circles, a sort of \"log revolution\" of that time.\n\nRotim confirms that everything that gathered around the Serbian cultural circle at that time went directly in the direction of dismembering Croatia, and the role intended for Croats is clearly described in the documents of the Chetnik movement of **Draža Mihailović**. He considers it very unfair to enter the context of the Second World War exclusively with April 10 and the arrival of National Socialist Germany and Fascist Italy. He points to the hypocrisy of the Western consciousness, which has never confronted the fact that it legitimized the Stalinist order, which up to **June 22, 1941**, was responsible for the death of millions of innocent people.\n\nExplaining the deeper reasons for the conflict, Rotim points out the different historical experience in relation to Turkish rule, which on the Serbian side produced political and cultural elites inclined toward conspiratorialism. Even the provisions of the agreement on the Banovina of Croatia, according to which districts with a Serbian majority would ultimately end up on the Serbian side, were not enough for the Belgrade elites; the goal was to reduce Croats to an enclave, while for Muslims, as numerically and militarily weaker, an even worse fate was planned. If the compromise politics of **Vladko Maček** were not enough — moreover, Croatian representatives were shot at in the Belgrade parliament — Rotim concludes that no reasonable person after that could claim that anything should be inherited from coexistence with Serbs.\n\nThe host and the guest then exhaustively list the key points of repression in the interwar period that preceded the collapse of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia:\n\n- **The December Victims (December 5, 1918)**, when the people in Zagreb rose up against the new order.\n- The political sobering up of the enthusiast **Ante Trumbić** in 1920 in Rapallo, when he realized that **Nikola Pašić** and the **Karađorđevićs** were handing over Croatian territories to Italy.\n- **The assassination in the Belgrade Assembly in 1928**, for which the host cites a personal experience from 2018 when in Belgrade, touring the Old and New Assembly, he realized that in the local historiography and space there is no marked trace of that crime whatsoever, while Rotim adds that the murderer **Puniša Račić** was released from prison as soon as the war events began.\n- The assassination of **King Alexander I**, the introduction of the January 6 Dictatorship, and the murders of around **three thousand Croats** from Lika to Hercegovina committed by Serbian gendarmes.",

     "subtitle": "The complex context of the establishment of the NDH, cultural life, and the suffering of Jews",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim analyzes the internal circumstances at the establishment of the Independent State of Croatia and the attitude toward racial laws.",
     "content": "To the host's question about the advantages and disadvantages of the **Independent State of Croatia (NDH)**, which according to the words of **Franjo Tuđman** was created also as an expression of the historical aspiration of the Croatian people for their own statehood, Rotim answers in layers. He points out that the establishment of the NDH in April 1941 happened across the country — through the Bjelovar uprising, the takeover of power in Zagreb, Podravina towns, Hercegovina, Dalmatia, and Slunj — whereby the Yugoslav army was disarmed before the very arrival of the Germans, without civilian casualties and without revenge.\n\nSpeaking about the internal life of the state, Rotim states that, despite wartime circumstances and the fact that the Ustaše tried to ideologically take over all the reins of power, a certain spiritual and cultural awakening occurred: books were printed, Croatian history was written about, Croatian identity was lived, and the Catholic faith was freely professed, while political Orthodoxy as a project of the Karađorđevićs no longer had its former power. However, he immediately moves on to the negative aspects as well, pointing out that Orthodox Christians were at one point outlawed, until they were called Greek-Easterners by the official authorities.\n\nRotim emphasizes that it is necessary to strictly separate the question of the suffering of Jews from the Serbian question in Croatia, because the Serbian side cunningly mixes those two questions in order to push itself into the victimology of the Holocaust. Speaking about the attitude toward Jews and the passing of racial laws, he presents several key points:\n\n- In the entirety of Europe at that time, there was a strong anti-Jewish spirit, which in some segments differed from the German racial-biological teaching, but created fertile ground for persecutions.\n- Although Croatian nationalist thought had earlier shown tolerance toward Jews (the host notes the presence of Jews in the movement ever since **Josip Frank**), Rotim, for the sake of historical truth, also mentions how the main magazine of the Jewish community in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia supported the policy of King Alexander to reduce Croats to the level of a tribe.\n- The passing of racial legislation in April and May 1941 was justified in the circles of that time as an attempt to replicate German laws so that the NDH authorities would get closer to the Germans and thereby obtain a more favorable position in the upcoming difficult negotiations with **Benito Mussolini** and the Italians over living space in Dalmatia and Istria.\n- Mussolini recognized the NDH with the caveat that the borders still had to be negotiated, which proves that **Ante Pavelić** in emigration had not promised or sold Dalmatia to him in advance.\n\nDespite these geopolitical calculations and the fact that the implementation of the laws was not equally comprehensive across the entire territory, Rotim and the host clearly conclude that the Holocaust, deportations, and racial laws cannot be justified in any way. A large part of the Jewish community was deported to **Auschwitz**, and that is a heavy fact with which the Croatian national and collective conscience must confront itself.",

     "subtitle": "The Belgrade coup of March 27, 1941, and closed archives in Serbia",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim calls for the opening of Belgrade archives, which hold over 500 boxes of material from the NDH period.",
     "content": "In order to further illuminate the events that preceded April 10, 1941, the host returns the chronology to **March 27, 1941**, and the military coup of General **Dušan Simović** in Belgrade. He reminds that immediately before that, the Yugoslav ambassador in Berlin, Nobel laureate **Ivo Andrić**, approached **Adolf Hitler** and conveyed Belgrade's decision on the accession of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia to the Tripartite Pact. When British agents launched demonstrations in Belgrade on March 27, Yugoslav historiography for decades showed only a cropped photograph with the slogan *\"Better pact than war\"* (that is, *\"Better war than pact\"*). However, the host states that during his studies in England and America, in institutes such as the **Smithsonian** in Washington, he saw the complete, uncropped photograph from those demonstrations: in it, Chetniks are seen with banners calling for a march on Croatia, the destruction and burning of the Banovina of Croatia. He concludes that, had the bombing of Belgrade not occurred, Serbian forces would have already then set out into a military showdown with the Banovina of Croatia.\n\nRotim follows up with the information that the Slovak ambassador in Belgrade also reported after the coup of March 27 that, observing Orthodox priests on the streets, the whole event did not look like Yugoslav resistance, but like the restoration of Greater Serbia. He also reminds of the warnings of the Croatian Club of Representatives after the murders in the Belgrade Assembly: the radicalization of the political scene was a direct consequence of the terror of gendarmes who since 1918 had beaten and killed people across Croatia without any accountability, while the families of the victims even had to pay for the bullets with which their loved ones were killed. Unlike Austria-Hungary, where problems were solved at the table, Croatia found itself opposite elites and the **Serbian Orthodox Church** who had been conspiratorially working on the unification of all Serbs since the 19th century.\n\nThis anti-Croatian activity continued immediately after April 10, 1941, before the first civilian victims fell:\n\n- **Niko Novaković Longo** from Dalmatia sends a petition to the Italians demanding the secession of Dalmatia under the pretext of the endangerment of Serbs.\n- In Belgrade, the introduction of military administration over the NDH is demanded from the Germans.\n- A special research question for historians is represented by the role of the German intelligence community and SS members in creating the atmosphere and \"horror propaganda\" in the first months of the NDH.\n\nIn doing so, Rotim directly addresses critics from Serbia who had insulted him in the preceding days on the social network X for commenting on **Lordan Zafranović**. He invites them to walk a few hundred meters to the Belgrade archives, which remain inaccessible to Croatian historians. Over **500 boxes of NDH material** are located there, including the minutes of the sessions of the Deputy Council and the Main Ustaša Headquarters, and he challenges them to finally pull out concrete documents that would incriminate **Alojzije Stepinac** or prove the alleged genocidal policy from the first months of the state.",

     "subtitle": "The rebellion in Srb, ethnic cleansing of Croats, and care for refugee children",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim speaks about the consequences of the rebellion in Srb in 1941, the suffering of civilians, and the care for refugee children.",
     "content": "The conversation moves on to the escalation of the conflict in the summer of 1941. The host points out that the events of **July 27, 1941, in Srb** and what followed until October of that year in the tri-border area do not have the character of a Partisan uprising, but represent a rebellion against any kind of Croatian state and classic ethnic cleansing with elements of genocide, in which Partisans and Chetniks collaborated with the Italians.\n\nRotim explains how the first two months of the NDH passed in the consolidation of power and the disarming of the Yugoslav army without mass shootings — in April and May 1941 there is nothing like the Katyn forest or the later communist crime in Tezno. However, former Yugoslav soldiers of Serbian nationality who returned to their homes refused for months to hand over their weapons. From the diaries, collections of papers, and memoirs of communists, for example those from **Drvar**, it is clearly seen that the July rebellion was carefully planned. When they assessed that they were ready, they did not attack the Ustaša garrison in Gospić, but set out into mass attacks on Croatian and Muslim civilians.\n\nThe consequences of that rebellion were catastrophic:\n\n- Entire Catholic parishes, such as those in **Bosansko Grahovo**, **Boričevac**, **Vrtoče**, and **Krnjeuša**, were completely eradicated and wiped off the face of the earth.\n- Horrific crimes were committed, such as the massacre of the Croatian **Ivezić** family, where children of just a few years of age were thrown alive into a pit.\n- A space was created to which Croatian authorities and the Croatian people no longer had access — a sort of \"SAO Krajina before SAO Krajina\".\n\nRotim particularly emphasizes that it was precisely the rebellion in Srb that caused the first major humanitarian catastrophe to hit children in the Second World War in these areas, which is a topic that directly precedes later manipulations around the children of Kozara. Columns of women and children fled from Boričevac and surrounding places toward **Bihać**, while Chetniks shot at the civilian refugee column and killed people. Despite difficult wartime conditions, food shortages, and constant sabotage by rebels on railway lines that were crucial for supply, the institutions of the NDH organized the reception of those refugees. The state placed children who were left without parents into homes and foster families, making no distinction whatsoever between Croatian and Muslim children.",

     "subtitle": "The Treaties of Rome, the question of Dalmatia, and chaotic power relations on the ground",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim explains the military pressure of Italy, the signing of the Treaties of Rome, and their annulment in September 1943.",
     "content": "Looking back at the negative aspects of the NDH, the host opens the painful question of the **Treaties of Rome** and the handing over of Dalmatia to Italy, pointing out that **Split**, together with Istria, was thrown into the hands of Italian fascists, which naturally spurred a strong resistance movement in those regions. He asks why the agreed dual, Italian-Croatian authority never came to life in Split.\n\nRotim answers that **Benito Mussolini** simply did not adhere to any agreements. After defeats in the African colonies, Italian fascist predators looked for space for the expansion of their planned Roman Empire, and on Croatian territory they had as many as **200 thousand soldiers** stationed. Precisely that huge military pressure was the second \"millstone\" around the neck of the young state that forced the Treaties of Rome. Rotim considers that in those negotiations as much was achieved as could be at that moment, noting that **Ante Pavelić** invited champions of Croatian national thought such as **Edo Bulat** into the negotiating team. Nevertheless, anti-Italian sentiment among the people was huge and was felt even in the public speeches of NDH officials, but Croatia was militarily too weak for an open conflict with Italy.\n\nAs soon as conditions were met, after the capitulation of Italy on **September 10, 1943**, the Treaties of Rome were terminated, and Dalmatia was returned to the composition of the NDH. Rotim reminds of the legal analysis by the jurist **Tihomir Drezga**, published in the newspapers of that time, in which it was elaborated in detail how those treaties were signed under duress and without good will, and how the Italian side had not adhered to them from the very beginning.\n\nDescribing the chaotic nature on the ground, especially south of the Sava where the strength of Croatian institutions and the army was questionable, Rotim points out that in the general state of war there was much improvisation:\n\n- The Italians collaborated with the Chetniks against the Croatian state from the very beginning.\n- From 1942, in strategically important northwestern Bosnia, even the NDH authorities concluded agreements with certain Chetnik groups, because the Chetnik movement was not unified.\n- On the ground, paradoxical relations prevailed in which sometimes the Black Legion helped the Partisans, the Partisans collaborated with the Italians, and the Italians with the Chetniks — everyone with everyone, because no one had a sufficient projection of military power to completely master the space.\n\nConcluding the first part of the conversation, Rotim emphasizes that one should clearly separate the concept of the Croatian state from Ustaša rule and unnecessary reprisals. He considers that the NDH authorities, especially in the summer of 1941, should and could have done more to suppress the acts of revenge and retaliations that followed after Serbian attacks. Regardless of who started first, he points out that every human being has a right to dignity and that there is no place for revenge — which is a lesson from history that, as the host notices, **Franjo Tuđman** learned very well, insisting in 1990 and 1991 on a policy of reconciliation and the prevention of any revanchism.",

   "theme": "The children of Kozara, deconstruction of myths about children's camps, and criticism of Lordan Zafranović's film",

     "subtitle": "The offensive on Kozara and the real causes of the humanitarian catastrophe of 1942",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim explains the causes of the armed rebellion on Kozara and the taking of children into the forest.",
     "content": "Continuing the conversation about the war events of 1941 and 1942, the host points out that in that period an exceptionally confusing situation prevailed on the territory of the Independent State of Croatia, while in Serbia at the same time peace prevailed without a significant Partisan movement. Looking back at the fate of the children from Kozara, the host cites the datum that over two thousand children were received into Croatian families, while in Belgrade only twenty were received, noting that children from a train going toward Serbia were returned with the explanation that they \"stink\", after which they were again cared for in Croatian families.\n\nOpening the topic of responsibility for the suffering of the youngest, the host asks a key question about the causes of that tragedy: what leads parents to take their own children, lead them into the forest, and with weapons in their hands go to war against the state in which they live, against the Germans, the Croatian army, and tanks? Historian **Krešimir Rotim** agrees that in public discourse exclusively the consequences of the humanitarian catastrophe are constantly observed, while its real causes are completely ignored.\n\nAccording to Rotim's words, the roots of that tragedy lie in successful communist agitation and general hostility toward the Croatian state. On the territory of Kozara, the rebels created a sort of \"SAO Krajina before SAO Krajina\", from where they systematically sabotaged railways and killed civilians. Because of the strategic importance of that area, a joint military offensive of German and Croatian troops was launched in order to suppress the rebellion. In doing so, Rotim reminds of the decree of Poglavnik **Ante Pavelić** on clearing rebel places ahead of the Kozara offensive. Despite the way Serbian and part of Croatian historiography portray Pavelić, Rotim points out that for the wartime conditions of that time, that decree was humanitarian because it explicitly ordered care for women and children, while the fight was waged exclusively against armed rebels. He therefore sees the main cause of the humanitarian catastrophe precisely in the parents who, armed to the teeth, led their own children into an armed rebellion.",

     "subtitle": "Systematic care for children: Archival cards, Diana Budisavljević, and the role of Caritas",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim speaks about 27 thousand cards in the Croatian State Archives that document the saving of children.",
     "content": "After the collapse of the rebellion on Kozara, thousands of children were initially placed in the vicinity of the Jasenovac camp and nearby places. When news of their catastrophic condition reached Zagreb, an extensive action of care was launched through state homes and families, following a similar procedure to that earlier applied for children from Bihać and its surroundings after the rebellion in Srb on July 27. **Krešimir Rotim** emphasizes that the entire process is documented in detail and that over **27 thousand cards** are kept in the **Croatian State Archives**, whereby every child has their first and last name recorded, data about their parents, and exact information on whether they ended up in a home or were fostered into a family. Despite that, Rotim adds, accusations still come from Serbia today that those children were forcibly converted to Catholicism, which he calls the Serbian \"industry of historical memories\" that cannot match exact historical documents.\n\nThe host follows up with a review of the film portrayal of the activity of **Diana Budisavljević**, pointing out that she was factually a great woman, but warns that in the public the key role of **Caritas of the Archdiocese of Zagreb** and Archbishop **Alojzije Stepinac** is completely minimized. He points to the absurdity of the narrative in which the Ustaša authorities and Stepinac are portrayed as absolute bloodthirsty killers in a fascist state, while at the same time it is claimed that Diana Budisavljević alone pulled out and cared for ten thousand children without anyone from the system seeing or hearing it. The host assesses such theses as completely irrational, emphasizing that Caritas stood strongly in the background of the entire rescue action and that Stepinac himself was deeply involved in everything and actively reacted.",

    {
     "subtitle": "Shelters in Sisak and Jastrebarsko versus the myth of children's camps",
     "screenshot_description": "Krešimir Rotim refutes myths about camps for children and presents data on the work of shelters.",
     "content": "One of the heaviest accusations that has been coming from Belgrade for decades, which the host calls a horrific and deranged policy of building hatred on the sacrifice of one's own children, is the claim that the NDH was the only state in the world that had camps for children in which nuns killed the youngest. **Krešimir Rotim** resolutely rejects such constructions, pointing out that there was no question of any camps, but rather **shelters for children** in **Sisak**, **Zagreb**, **Jastrebarsko**, **Gornja Rijeka**, and other places.\n\nAs an illustrative example of the conduct of the authorities of that time, Rotim cites a document ordered by **Maks Luburić** by which eight hundred Kozara children and mothers are sent to **Požega** and its surroundings. Because of the general wartime food shortage in all areas, Luburić orders in the document that the local Orthodox families feed them. Rotim points out that this is the only \"offense\" that can be found in that context and that there is no talk of gas chambers or systematic killing. Numerous church and state documents, as well as testimonies of nuns, testify to the catastrophic and starved condition in which the children arrived from the forest. Rotim wonders how it is possible that a part of the public in Croatia believes that every single individual in the system of that time – from **Kamilo Bresler** from the Red Cross to employees of the Ministry of Health – were fascists and enemies of Serbian infants.\n\nIn support of this, he also cites the testimony of **Ante Dumbović**, an employee of the shelter in Sisak, who in 1945 or 1946 before a communist court – along with the inevitable politically correct phrases of that time – clearly described what a difficult condition the children were brought in and in what way they were cared for. Speaking about the mortality rate of children in those shelters, Rotim presents the datum that it ranged between **20 and 30 percent**, which, given the difficult wartime conditions and diseases, is even lower compared to some other post-war periods, such as the great famine and shortage in the SFRY in 1945 and 1946 when mortality in certain segments reached even 50 percent. Accusing nuns and employees of the Ministry of Health of receiving instructions for starving and killing children is, for Rotim, pure slander that exists only in someone's imagination.",
